A quality criterion can restrict bank admission in addition to correctness
and canonical validity. Examples include a token budget, a process-reward
threshold, or a trace-quality classifier; a quality score could also guide
exemplar selection within a key or eviction at capacity. These changes
alter the replay target and are not part of the uniform-replay comparison.
Quality and diversity can conflict when alternative modes require longer
solutions. \texttt{MathIR} alternatives include trajectories through additional
states, and \texttt{Python}'s rarer return vectors require longer lambdas than its
modal vector. A brevity filter can therefore remove valid alternatives;
diversity is measured after applying the filter.
after:
Additional quality criteria, such as a token budget or trace-quality score,
would change admission, exemplar selection, or eviction and hence the replay
target. They are not used in these comparisons. A brevity filter can remove
valid alternatives: \texttt{MathIR} includes longer state trajectories, and
\texttt{Python}'s rarer return vectors require longer lambdas than its modal
vector. Any such filter would need evaluation of both solution quality and
diversity among the retained modes.

before:
Each exact prompt-token sequence has an independent count table. Counts
include only responses with positive task reward and a valid canonical
key; invalid and unsuccessful responses affect neither the predictor nor
its history. Counts accumulate throughout training, with no window, decay,
eviction, or reset. Each eligible response is scored against the preceding groups'
counts and its own successful leave-one-out peers. The current group's
counts are added after all its responses have been scored, so a response
never contributes to its own predictor.
after:
Counts are maintained separately for each exact prompt-token sequence and
accumulate throughout training without decay or reset. Only responses with
positive reward and a valid key contribute. Each response is scored using
preceding groups and its successful leave-one-out peers; the current group
is added afterward. A response therefore never contributes to its own
predictor.
